newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk president to meet Yilmaz in coalition talks.
newsitem.headline: Turk president to meet Yilmaz in coalition talks.

text.p: Turkish President Suleyman Demirel invited main opposition figure Mesut Yilmaz to his residence on Friday amid speculation the Motherland Party leader would be asked to head a new "Islamist-free" government.
State-run Anatolian news agency said Demirel would hold talks with Yilmaz at 5 p.m. (1400 GMT).
It gave no more details of the meeting, their second meeting in two days.
Yilmaz, a staid conservative, is one of the favourites to be appointed by Demirel as prime minister-designate following the resignation of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.
Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader, stepped down on Wednesday after months of pressure from the secularist military.
He asked Demirel to approve a plan under which pro-Western Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller would head a new coalition with the Islamists to take Turkey to early elections.
But the Turkish media said the president did not favour Ciller, Erbakan's ally in an odd couple coalition since last June.
"The president does not want to give priority to Ciller," the Hurriyet daily quoted sources close to Demirel as saying.
"If he had wanted to do that he would not have wasted Turkey's time. He would have asked her to form a new government as soon as Erbakan resigned," one unnamed source said.
Another mainstream newspaper carried similar quotes.
Yilmaz, prime minister twice since 1991, went to Ankara's main Kocatepe mosque for Friday prayers after Demirel's invitation, party sources said.
He was confident he could head a government that would get past a parliamentary vote of confidence.
"There is an extremely high possibility that a government formed under me can win a vote of confidence," he told the NTV television news channel late on Thursday night.
The leaders of two leftist parties said after a series of meetings with Demirel on Thursday that they would support conservative Yilmaz in parliament.
But the planned secularist alliance would still need backing from a small right-wing group and around a dozen defections from Ciller's True Path Party to forge a feasible government.

Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, is distrusted by many in the secularist establishment for going into coalition with Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party, after pledging not to do so.
"Certain forces...are openly making propaganda aimed at turning Turkey into a state based on religion," said Bulent Eczacibasi, a ceramics and pharmacy tycoon.
"We have seen coalition partners doing nothing to stop these efforts, and in fact supporting them," he told a meeting of the TUSIAD industrialists' group in Istanbul.
The president's press office said in a statement that he would meet armed forces chief General Ismail Hakki Karadayi later on Friday for what it called a regular meeting.
The army has a long history of intervention in politics, deposing three governments in the last four decades.
Top commanders have branded religious activism as "public enemy number one" and last week made a veiled threat to use force to halt the Islamists.
A handful of anti-Islamist True Path deputies have said they would not vote for Ciller as prime minister in any new coalition that kept the Islamists in office.

But a long-awaited party rebellion against Ciller has yet to come about and analysts say potential renegades fear losing their place on the party's lists at early elections if they challenge their leader.
